pages.text:
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE, Plaintiff, v. KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6, Defendants. ____________________________________/ | Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION UNDER RULE 26(d)(1) FOR PRESENT AUTHORIZATION TO SERVE TWO INTERROGATORIES ON META CONCERNING PLAINTIFF’S FULL LEGAL NAME AND FACEBOOK ACCOUNT

I.	INTRODUCTION

“If you deserve the hammer, you’re getting the hammer.” Here, in Ballentine v. Hall, et al., there is a man who either deserves the hammer or a man who deserves the right to clear his name.

There are either CyberTipline reports that connect Marvelle J. Ballentine to the most vile type of human conduct imaginable, or there are not.

Should documents exist that connect Marvelle J. Ballentine to the most heinous type of conduct a human being can engage in, and should those documents establish that he committed such conduct, then Marvelle J. Ballentine should get the hammer. It should include, if warranted by law, permanent separation from society, as well as prompt and immediate dismissal of this action.

If no such report exists, then Marvelle J. Ballentine deserves to vindicate his name and begin the process of reintegration into his personal and professional networks.

Before the Court decides which man is before it, consider what the letters did to him.

Imagine receiving two letters that indicate evidence may exist connecting you with the lowest form of human life — individuals who commit crimes against children.

Imagine your own wife reading the letters. Imagine the look of deep concern in her eyes as she turns toward her own children.

Imagine the flashbacks to your own trauma. Imagine the tears shed while hunched over a toilet bowl.

Imagine telling your wife it’s OK if she got on a plane and took the kids to stay at the in-laws, and that you would understand if she did not return.

Imagine drafting Rule 41 dismissal notices, printing them out, and — with tears flowing — being a little boy in a church pew again, hearing the booming voice of your grandfather from the pulpit: “You told me in your word, in a time of distress, if I call on you, you’d hear my cry!”

Then imagine saying to yourself: “Don’t cry to give up. Cry to keep going.”

Then imagine proceeding.

Marvelle J. Ballentine proceeded. Meta says the letters are the exact discovery. Plaintiff says show it. Meta refuses. Plaintiff asks the Court for four interrogatories. Denied as premature. Plaintiff asks for a Rule 26(f) conference. Denied. Plaintiff asks for a Rule 16(b) scheduling order. Denied. All three requests are denied while Meta seeks dismissal with prejudice. The Court may now dismiss the case, leaving Plaintiff’s sons to wonder whether their father’s name ever appeared in a report concerning the sexual exploitation of children.

The answer has been pursued in courts from the East Coast to the West Coast, against resistance from the defense and from the Courts. That resistance serves no one — least of all children — if Mr. Ballentine is a predator.

This Court knows what the hammer means. On September 23, 2026, Judge Alston sentenced a man to eighteen years in prison for attempted sexual exploitation of a child arising from communications initiated on Facebook. United States v. Bonilla Canales, No. 1:26-cr-00004-RDA, ECF No. __ (E.D. Va. Sept. 23, 2026). The Court sat as factfinder, heard that evidence, and found it proved. Id., ECF No. 59 at 1, 3–4. Should evidence ever warrant prosecuting Mr. Ballentine for such conduct, he may one day stand in this very courtroom to receive the hammer. Today he stands before the same Court asking whether the reports invoked against his name even identify him. The Court that imposes eighteen years for crimes proved can order two sworn answers for a man trying to clear his name. If the defense is unable to supply the report, then substitute the pen for the hammer.

The pen should say: “The motion is granted.”

II.	EITHER POSSIBILITY FAVORS AN ANSWER

Assume the worst. Assume that Marvelle J. Ballentine committed crimes against children and that the reports contain evidence of it. Children deserve protection. He deserves accountability. Now assume that the association is baseless. Then he has a name to clear. Either possibility favors getting the facts right. The man asking for those facts is Marvelle J. Ballentine.

Meta describes the discovery Plaintiff sought in Florida as “whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff,” and his notice to NCMEC as concerning “whether a CyberTipline report . . . was filed in connection with the Facebook account associated with Plaintiff and terminated on or about July 4, 2022.” ECF No. 22 at 4. Meta describes the April 22 letters as “the exact discovery that Hall and NCMEC provided.” Id. at 9. The letters name no provider and no account. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3; FAC ¶¶ 91–92. Meta has told the Court that two letters which do not mention Meta or the account answered whether Meta reported the account. One party can know whether that is so. Meta has not said what it submitted. Plaintiff has received no correspondence from NCMEC indicating a law-enforcement referral and no law-enforcement contact concerning the matters addressed in the April 22 letters. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 17. He has the letters. He lives with the association. He is still asking for the facts.

If Meta answers “Yes” to Interrogatory No. 1, it submitted a report, between July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, that contained the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine” as submitted. That report went to NCMEC. NCMEC makes each report available to law enforcement. 18 U.S.C. § 2258A(c). A sworn “Yes” discloses to Plaintiff nothing the statute has not already placed within reach of a federal agency. On that answer, Plaintiff has the fact he has sought since October 2025.

If Meta answers “Yes” to Interrogatory No. 2, it submitted a report in connection with the account it enforced against on July 4, 2022. The letters omitted that fact. FAC ¶ 92. The account-discovery sequence pleaded in Counts IV and V has turned on that fact since October 2025. FAC ¶¶ 33, 35, 124–135.

If Meta answers “No” to both, Meta submitted no report containing the name and no report connected to the account. The letters then answered nothing about Meta. “Exact” described nothing Meta did. On that answer the remedy lies in this Court.

If Meta answers “Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry,” a provider has stated under oath that it cannot determine what it submitted about one account it enforced against. That is Meta’s present knowledge, sworn.

No answer discloses a report’s contents, a narrative, a third party, or an image. No answer requires production. No answer harms a child. Meta has identified no burden and no privilege. ECF No. 73 at 3–4. The one interest that delay serves is the sequence Meta proposes: dismissal first, discovery after. Id. at 4. Rule 26(d)(1) does not list that interest.

Meta is the provider. Meta knows what Meta submitted. Meta called the letters exact. Meta can say whether they were. Each answer places this action in a defined posture. The Court cannot assess that posture without the answer. Each answer is one word.

III.	META’S OWN FILINGS MAKE ITS POSITION INCOHERENT

Meta says the letters are the exact discovery of whether Meta reported. Meta says the letters do not say whether Meta reported. Meta says the answer has no bearing. Meta asks the Court to end the action on that record. Each statement is Meta’s. Each sits beside its opposite below.

Meta tells the Court | Meta tells the Court in the same filing

Meta moved on April 21, 2026 “to try to prevent the exact discovery that Hall and NCMEC provided on April 22, 2026.” ECF No. 22 at 9. | “despite Meta refusing to respond to similar discovery requests directed at it.” Id. at 2.

The Florida discovery concerned “whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff.” Id. at 4. | The letters “did not state that Meta . . . submitted either report, that either report concerned Plaintiff’s Facebook account.” Id. at 7 (quoting FAC ¶ 92).

NCMEC “provided him with exactly what he asked for, albeit allegedly prematurely.” Id. at 11. | “That is not a threat, it is professional courtesy.” Id.

“discovery that he himself requested.” Id. at 12. | “any discovery would have no bearing on the resolution of Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.” ECF No. 73 at 4.

Discovery should follow survival of the claims and the Rule 26(f) conference. Id. | “Meta respectfully requests that the Court dismiss the FAC with prejudice.” ECF No. 22 at 14.

A.	Meta’s refusal to answer in Florida is not the difficulty

Meta refused the account question in Florida. ECF No. 22 at 2. Meta moved on April 21, 2026 to stay the discovery that asked it. Id. at 9; FAC ¶¶ 64, 66. A party may oppose discovery directed at it. Plaintiff does not contest that. The difficulty is in what Meta then told the Court the letters were.

B.	Meta says the letters are the exact discovery of whether Meta reported

Meta describes the Florida discovery as “whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff.” ECF No. 22 at 4. Meta describes the April 22 letters as “the exact discovery that Hall and NCMEC provided on April 22, 2026.” Id. at 9. Meta describes the letters as “exactly what he asked for.” Id. at 11. “Exact” is a statement about content. The letters are the exact discovery of whether Meta reported the account only if Meta knows what it reported and knows that the letters describe it.

C.	Meta says the letters do not mention Meta or the account

Meta’s memorandum recites the FAC’s allegation that the letters “did not state that Meta . . . submitted either report, that either report concerned Plaintiff’s Facebook account, or that either report” concerned the account’s disablement. ECF No. 22 at 7 (quoting FAC ¶ 92). The letters name no provider and no account. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3; FAC ¶¶ 91–92. Page 7 of Meta’s memorandum states what the letters omit. Page 9 calls the letters exact. Page 11 calls them exactly what he asked for. The same memorandum carries all three pages.

D.	Meta says the answer has no bearing

Meta states that “any discovery would have no bearing on the resolution of Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.” ECF No. 73 at 4. Meta proposes discovery after the claims survive and the parties confer. Id. Meta identified no burden and no privilege. Id. at 3–4. Meta is the provider. Meta invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against the account on July 4, 2022. ECF No. 59-2 ¶ 3. A provider that obtains actual knowledge of an apparent violation reports it to the CyberTipline. 18 U.S.C. § 2258A(a)(1). Meta knows whether it made that report. Meta knows what name it put in it. Meta has stated that the letters are exact. Meta has not stated what it submitted. No Meta filing states that Meta submitted a report concerning the account. No Meta filing states that it did not.

E.	Meta asks the Court to end the action on that record

Meta “respectfully requests that the Court dismiss the FAC with prejudice.” ECF No. 22 at 14. The premises are Meta’s own. The letters are the exact discovery of whether Meta reported. Id. at 9. The letters do not say whether Meta reported. Id. at 7. Meta refused to say whether Meta reported. Id. at 2. The answer has no bearing. ECF No. 73 at 4. The conclusion Meta draws from those premises is dismissal with prejudice. ECF No. 22 at 14. Meta called the letters exact. Meta holds the fact that would make them so. Meta asks that the action end without stating it.

F.	The positions reconcile on one reading, and that reading loses the motion

Meta’s positions reconcile on one reading. On that reading “exact” describes the form of the letters, a response matching the schedule Plaintiff drafted, and not their content. On that reading Meta has told the Court nothing about whether Meta reported the account, and the two questions in Exhibit A remain open. Meta’s memorandum does not hold that reading. Meta’s argument at page 9 is that the FAC alleges “contradictory conduct” because Meta moved to prevent “the exact discovery” that NCMEC then provided. ECF No. 22 at 9. That argument works only if the letters supplied the content Meta moved to prevent. On the content reading, Meta has told the Court what its reports contain while declining to say so under oath. On the form reading, the conduct Meta calls contradictory is not contradictory, and the argument built on it falls. Either reading leaves the two questions unanswered.

G.	Two answers resolve it

Plaintiff asks for two interrogatories. Not the reports. Not their contents. Not a narrative. Two sworn answers: whether Meta submitted a report containing the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” and whether Meta submitted a report connected to the account it enforced against on July 4, 2022. Exhibit A permits three answers to each. Part II states what each answer establishes. Meta presently holds every position in the table above and none of the answers. The Court is asked to accept Meta’s description of the letters as exact and leave untested the one party that knows whether they were. Plaintiff asks for the facts.

IV.	THE ACCOUNT QUESTION PRECEDED THE LETTERS, AND THE LETTERS DID NOT ANSWER IT

The account question is older than the letters. Whether Meta, or anyone acting in connection with the July 4, 2022 account-enforcement event, transmitted a CyberTipline report concerning Plaintiff or his account identifiers has been contested since October 2025. ECF No. 5 (“FAC”) ¶ 33. Plaintiff’s first substantive act in the 376 Action was a motion for leave to serve one early request for admission on that question. FAC ¶ 35. Meta’s own memorandum describes that request and the later notice to NCMEC concerning “whether a CyberTipline report . . . was filed in connection with the Facebook account associated with Plaintiff and terminated on or about July 4, 2022.” ECF No. 22 at 4; see id. at 6.

On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff sent NCMEC’s Legal Department advance notice of two intended subpoenas, one for each Florida action, with signed drafts to be served after a notice period. ECF No. 7-6 at 2–3. The cover letter stated one subject: “whether a CyberTipline report under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A was filed concerning the Facebook account associated with Marvelle J. Ballentine and terminated on or about July 4, 2022.” Id.

On April 22, 2026, Hall signed two letters on NCMEC letterhead, one captioned to each action. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. Each states: “NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.” Id. The letters quote the three identifiers from Plaintiff’s April 9 notice. FAC ¶¶ 77–78. They identify no report number, report date, or reporting provider. FAC ¶ 91. They do not state that Meta submitted either report or that either report concerned Plaintiff’s Facebook account. FAC ¶ 92. They join the identifiers with “and/or” and do not say which identifier appeared in any submission. FAC ¶¶ 93, 96–97. Meta’s memorandum recites paragraph 92. ECF No. 22 at 7.

The two interrogatories address two different gaps. Interrogatory No. 1 asks whether Meta submitted, in the period the letters name, any CyberTipline report that contained Plaintiff’s full legal name as submitted. It is not limited to the account. Interrogatory No. 2 asks whether Meta submitted, in the same period, any CyberTipline report in connection with the account Meta enforced against on or about July 4, 2022. It carries no name condition. Either question can be answered without assuming an affirmative answer to the other.

V.	META HAS CHARACTERIZED THE LETTERS WITHOUT ANSWERING ITS OWN SUBMISSION QUESTIONS

Meta’s memorandum describes the letters twice. At page 9, Meta argues that the FAC “alleges contradictory conduct—namely, that Meta engaged in motion practice on April 21, 2026, to try to prevent the exact discovery that Hall and NCMEC provided on April 22, 2026.” ECF No. 22 at 9. At page 11, Meta argues that NCMEC “provided him with exactly what he asked for, albeit allegedly prematurely.” Id. at 11. Each sentence characterizes what the letters supplied. Neither states whether Meta submitted a report containing Plaintiff’s full legal name or a report connected to the enforced account. In the cited briefing, Meta has supplied no sworn statement on either submission question. Those questions remain unresolved. Part III sets out those descriptions beside Meta’s other statements.

Meta’s opposition to the earlier discovery motion adds three points. The FAC does not “plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy.” ECF No. 73 at 3. Discovery should follow survival of the claims and the Rule 26(f) conference. Id. at 4. And because the dismissal motion “tests only the sufficiency of the allegations in the FAC, any discovery would have no bearing on the resolution of Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.” Id. The third point concerns what the Court may consider on a Rule 12 motion, not whether the answers are relevant to pleaded claims. Part IX keeps those questions apart.

VI.	PLAINTIFF HAS SWORN TO THE ACCOUNT NAME HE USED

Plaintiff has sworn to his own naming practices. Before April 22, 2026, he never used “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any Meta account he used. ECF No. 31 ¶ 3. He never used that name as a username, profile name, display name, or account name on any Meta product. Id. ¶ 4. He did not provide that name to Meta as the name identifying him or any account. Id. ¶ 5. He used “Jay Ballentine.” Id. ¶ 6. The full name appeared in his April 9 materials because it is his legal name and the name in the case captions. Id. ¶¶ 7–8. On July 4, 2022, Meta invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against the Facebook account Plaintiff operated. ECF No. 59-2 ¶ 3. Plaintiff operated that account under the name “Jay Ballentine.” Id. ¶ 4. The enforcement action was not issued against an account operated under “Marvelle J. Ballentine.” Id. ¶ 5; see id. ¶¶ 6–10. Those sworn facts explain the two questions.

VII.	ORDINARY DISCOVERY HAS BEEN DEFERRED AT EACH STAGE, AND NEITHER QUESTION HAS BEEN ANSWERED

The deferral has a history. In the earlier 1341 Action, Plaintiff’s July 16, 2026 opposition reported that he had proposed Rule 26(f) planning on July 13 and had served no party discovery. Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, No. 1:26-cv-01341-MSN-WBP, ECF No. 13 at 2–3 (E.D. Va.). Hall and NCMEC moved on July 15 to stay discovery and Rule 26 obligations. Id., ECF No. 11 at 1, 3–4. On July 17, the court stayed discovery pending the dismissal motion. Id., ECF No. 15 at 1.

In this action, NCMEC stated that it would move to stay the Rule 26(f) requirement if Plaintiff sought a conference before its dismissal motion was decided. ECF No. 33 at 3. No separately docketed defense motion seeking that stay appears through ECF No. 136, filed November 9, 2026. On October 7, 2026, the Court denied Plaintiff’s earlier limited-discovery motions “as premature,” stating that discovery “officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2. On October 29, 2026, the Court stated that “the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. Those two orders, not the absence of a defense stay motion, define the present posture.

Meta itself invoked the earlier stay when it opposed the prior interrogatories, and it proposed discovery after the claims survive dismissal. ECF No. 73 at 4–5. Its own present argument supplies the connection.

On November 5, 2026, the Court directed that the motions previously set for December 16, 2026 be decided on the papers. Plaintiff independently waives argument on this application. The accompanying Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine (“Ballentine Decl.”) supplies the current consequences of the unresolved association, and the pending dismissal requests make clarification urgent while ordinary discovery remains deferred. Authorization does not depend on showing that a Rule 12 ruling requires additional evidence.

VIII.	ARGUMENT

A.	Rule 26(d)(1) Authorizes the Requested Order

Rule 26(d)(1) provides that a party “may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f), except . . . when authorized by these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” The rule states the bar and then states the exception. A court order lifts the bar. A scheduling order is not a textual prerequisite to that authority. Courts in this District apply the exception. Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. v. Markfeld, No. 3:25-cv-00885-RCY, ECF No. 70 at 17 (E.D. Va. July 29, 2026) (“Courts may allow discovery to begin before a Rule 26(f) conference occurs.”); Shenzhenshibairihongmaoyiyouxiangongsi v. Novoluto GmbH, No. 3:25-cv-00844-RCY, ECF No. 44 at 3 (E.D. Va. Mar. 9, 2026). The exercise of that authority is discretionary; district courts have “broad discretion to supervise discovery.” Gallagher, ECF No. 70 at 17. Plaintiff asks for an express, limited exception to the posture described in ECF No. 108.

B.	Plaintiff Asks the Court to Apply the Modified Preliminary-Injunction Test

Gallagher observed that “the Fourth Circuit has not established” a standard for expedited discovery and that courts in this District “apply a modified preliminary injunction test.” ECF No. 70 at 17. That test “looks to whether the Plaintiff has made a strong showing of merits and irreparable harm to Plaintiff in the absence of expedited discovery and is justified by the idea that granting court relief outside of the federal rules should be limited to unusual circumstances.” Id. at 17–18. Novoluto states the same test, premised on limiting relief outside the rules to “unusual circumstances.” ECF No. 44 at 3–4.

Plaintiff asks the Court to apply that test. These opinions supply the selected framework. They do not state a categorical rule binding every early-discovery request, and Plaintiff attributes none to the Fourth Circuit. Part VIII.G separately shows good cause under the additional approach courts in this District have used. The application follows: merits (Part VIII.C), irreparable harm (Part VIII.D), and unusual circumstances with tailoring (Parts VIII.E and VIII.F).

C.	The Merits Showing on Counts IV and V

The merits assessment requested here is preliminary and concerns this discovery application. Plaintiff seeks no final adjudication of liability in the authorization order. The chosen framework requires a merits assessment. The claims remain connected to the discovery.

Count IV. The first clause of 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) reaches a conspiracy to deter a party or witness in a court of the United States from attending that court or from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully. The deterrence must be by force, intimidation, or threat. Meta states the elements as “(1) a conspiracy, (2) to deter attendance in court or testimony by force or intimidation and (3) injury to the plaintiff.” ECF No. 22 at 9. The FAC pleads the understanding at ¶ 124. Between April 9 and April 22, 2026, Meta, through authorized representatives or intermediaries, and Hall, individually and as NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel, reached an understanding. Hall would issue correspondence asserting the existence of CyberTipline reports before service of the intended subpoenas and while motions directed at the same discovery remained pending. Id. The FAC pleads the purpose at ¶¶ 158–159. The purpose was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from attending the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party. It was also to deter him from testifying as a prospective witness about his account and the enforcement event. Id. The count is stated at ¶¶ 234–242 and the injury at ¶¶ 169–180. Plaintiff’s declaration supplies the historical participation effect: the letters led him to seriously contemplate his continued participation in the Florida proceedings. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 4. The current effects appear at ¶¶ 10–16.

The pleaded basis for the understanding is a sequence. As of April 9, 2026, NCMEC and counsel for Meta had received identical materials identifying the same two actions, the same three identifiers, and the same discovery objective. FAC ¶¶ 58–59, 126. On April 21, 2026, Meta joined motions to stay discovery in both actions, directed at the same discovery. FAC ¶¶ 64, 66, 127. The depositions covering the report-existence question were set for April 28 through 30. FAC ¶ 128. Hall and NCMEC were under no compulsory obligation. FAC ¶ 129. One day after the motions, and before the stated notice period ran, Hall issued two letters, each bearing the caption of one action. FAC ¶¶ 130–131. The letters asserted that reports exist. They omitted the provider, dates, numbers, matched identifier, platform, account connection, and disposition. They supplied, outside discovery, an unsworn assertion on the subject noticed for sworn examination. FAC ¶¶ 132–135. The inference rests on five facts together: common receipt; motions aimed at the same discovery; no obligation; two case-keyed instruments one day later; and an unsworn assertion in place of sworn examination.

Meta’s own descriptions identify the relationship. Meta describes its April 21 motion practice and the April 22 letters as directed at “the exact discovery.” ECF No. 22 at 9; see id. at 11. Part III.F addresses the reading on which that characterization rests. That discovery was the account question. Id. at 4, 6. The letters did not say whether Meta submitted a report connected to that account. FAC ¶ 92. Meta’s descriptions support examining the relationship between the requested account information and what the letters supplied.

Meta’s meeting-of-the-minds objection is this: the FAC alleges “parallel conduct and a bare assertion of conspiracy,” indeed “contradictory conduct,” and the Fourth Circuit has “rarely, if ever, found that a plaintiff has set forth sufficient facts to establish a section 1985 conspiracy.” ECF No. 22 at 9 (quoting Simmons v. Poe, 47 F.3d 1370, 1377 (4th Cir. 1995)). The FAC does not rest on a label. It pleads the dated sequence above and identifies the facts on which the understanding rests. FAC ¶¶ 124–135. Plaintiff asks the Court to draw the inference of agreement from that sequence. Meta opposed the account discovery in court on April 21. The next day, NCMEC supplied, outside any process, an assertion on the same subject. That assertion answered the noticed question without exposing any witness to examination. Lowy v. Daniel Defense, LLC, 167 F.4th 175, 199 (4th Cir. 2026), supports properly grounded information-and-belief pleading. The requested answers would establish whether Meta made a qualifying submission, the fact on which the account-discovery sequence has turned since October 2025.

Count V. Virginia common-law conspiracy requires a combination of two or more persons to accomplish an unlawful purpose, or a lawful purpose by unlawful means, and an actionable underlying tort. Meta frames the count the same way. ECF No. 22 at 14. The FAC pleads the combination, the means, the intended third-party publication, the overt acts, intent, and damages. FAC ¶¶ 245–250; see id. ¶¶ 243–251. Count V is not a second § 1985 count. Its predicates are the two letters and the person-level defamatory meaning they are alleged to convey. The FAC pleads publication through the commercial mail channel. FAC ¶¶ 184–186, 205–207. It pleads identification of Plaintiff by his full legal name. Id. ¶¶ 187, 208. It pleads defamatory meaning per se and by implication. Id. ¶¶ 188–190, 209–211. It pleads falsity. Id. ¶¶ 191, 212. It pleads fault from negligence through actual malice. Id. ¶¶ 192–194, 213–215.

Meta argues that the predicate torts fail under the litigation privilege and 18 U.S.C. § 2258D. ECF No. 22 at 14. Each defense is met here.

Litigation privilege. Meta argues that the defamation claims “are barred by the litigation privilege because Plaintiff’s claims seek to impose liability based on information contained in a response to subpoenas.” ECF No. 22 at 14. Virginia’s absolute privilege can reach qualifying communications made outside the courtroom, including certain communications preliminary to contemplated litigation. Mansfield v. Bernabei, 284 Va. 116, 122, 124–25, 727 S.E.2d 69 (2012). The question is whether these letters, as pleaded, fall within it. The FAC alleges advance notice of intended subpoenas, no served process, no court order, and no request for an early answer. It alleges letters addressed to Plaintiff alone and filed with no tribunal. It alleges a purpose to deter his participation. FAC ¶¶ 70–80, 158–162; see ECF No. 20 at 4–5. The letters’ express reference to the two actions is part of the context. So is the absence of any served subpoena. On the pleaded facts the predicate for the privilege is not established.

Statutory protection. Meta invokes § 2258D for the NCMEC predicate. ECF No. 22 at 14. NCMEC’s own briefing also invokes 34 U.S.C. § 20505. ECF No. 11 at 7. Section 2258D(a) turns on whether the claim arises from the performance of NCMEC’s designated CyberTipline responsibilities or functions. Subsection (b) withdraws protection for intentional misconduct and for a purpose unrelated to the designated functions. It also withdraws protection for actual malice or reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification. Subsection (c) excludes ordinary business activity. Section 20505 reaches specified reputational claims arising from communications in connection with a clearinghouse, hotline, or intake program. It yields where the plaintiff shows actual malice or a purpose unrelated to an activity mandated by federal law. The two statutes have different scopes and different exceptions. Neither statute’s exceptions transfer to the other. The FAC pleads that neither letter was a CyberTipline report, a referral, or any reporting, preservation, or disclosure function. It pleads that each letter was voluntary correspondence issued without any served subpoena or order. FAC ¶ 80. It pleads, in the alternative, the knowing false invocation of process, the wording Hall selected, and the knowledge or reckless disregard from which actual malice is inferred. FAC ¶¶ 192–194, 213–215. Those allegations go to the function and purpose on which each statute turns. Neither statute protects Meta on its own account merely because Meta is a provider. Each is asserted for the NCMEC predicate.

The two questions have a precise role. Interrogatory No. 1 tests whether Meta made any qualifying submission containing the full legal name. Interrogatory No. 2 tests the account-reporting relationship at the center of the pleaded sequence. Neither asks Meta to search for a conspiracy or for every communication among Defendants. The showing rests on the pleaded sequence, Meta’s own identification of the shared discovery subject, the sworn naming declarations, the letters’ omissions, and the responses above to the asserted defenses. That record satisfies the merits requirement stated in Part VIII.B.

D.	The Unresolved Association Causes Continuing Harm

1.	The injury already exists. The association between Plaintiff’s full legal name and two CyberTipline reports is already in the public litigation record. The letters use the listed names and email with “and/or.” ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. Hall and NCMEC attached the letters to their June 16, 2026 dismissal memorandum in the 1341 Action. ECF No. 7-2 at 2, 14, 16. Plaintiff later reproduced the letters here. ECF No. 7-1 ¶¶ 2, 5; ECF No. 7-5. NCMEC defends the letters as accurate. ECF No. 11 at 9; ECF No. 74 at 5. Meta describes them as the discovery Plaintiff requested. ECF No. 22 at 9, 11.

Plaintiff has never seen a CyberTipline report. He does not know whether any original report contains his full legal name. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 5–6. The public assertion remains while its original-report identification remains unknown to him. Plaintiff cites the filing history to explain present exposure and uncertainty. Consistent with FAC ¶ 26, he predicates no new claim on a court filing.

Plaintiff previously experienced a refusal of legal services that he understood to be attributable at least partly to his account’s child-sexual-exploitation designation. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 8. His September 2025 complaint recorded the representation obstacle before the letters existed. Id. ¶ 9 & Ex. 1; Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:25-cv-07671, ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 11–12 at 3 (N.D. Cal.). The experience explains the present concern.

2.	The injury has continuing consequences. Plaintiff intends to retain counsel for his pending litigation so that he can devote more attention to Docket Entry and his family. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 10. The earlier refusal makes him reluctant to risk another rejection while the association remains unresolved. E.	Unusual Circumstances Make Present Authorization Warranted

Four features combine. The declaration establishes current consequences. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 10–16. They are the intended retention of counsel, the restriction on open professional participation, the effect on daily work and family, and the use of accurate sworn information in present decisions. F.	The Two Questions Are Relevant and Proportional

Both questions are relevant. Rule 26(b)(1) permits discovery of nonprivileged matter “relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case.” Both questions go to the account-discovery sequence pleaded in Counts IV and V and to Meta’s descriptions of the letters. FAC ¶¶ 33, 35, 124–135, 234–251; ECF No. 22 at 4, 9, 11. Interrogatory No. 1 concerns any qualifying Meta submission containing the full name. The request is proportional. It limits disclosure to two answers about one full name and one specified account during July 1, 2022 through April 22, 2026, inclusive. It requires no report production, no search of all communications, no narrative, no report number, no date, and no submitter identity. The full-name question is not limited to the specified account or to the two letters. Meta’s characterization of NCMEC’s response does not establish that Meta has already completed either search. Under Rule 26(b)(1), the pleaded interests are the claims in Counts IV and V and the present consequences in Part VIII.D. Plaintiff lacks access, Meta controls its own submission records, and a defined answer resolves or narrows the stated question. Plaintiff requests seven days because the disclosure is confined and concerns Meta’s own defined submission records. G.	Good Cause Independently Supports This Limited Authorization

Courts in this District have also authorized limited identifying discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference on a showing of good cause. Strike 3 Holdings, LLC v. Doe, No. 1:25-cv-01308-MSN-WBP, ECF No. 7 at 2–3 (E.D. Va. Aug. 21, 2025). Strike 3 concerned a subpoena to an internet service provider to identify an unknown copyright defendant for service. Id. It considered a concrete actionable claim, the specificity of the request, the absence of alternative means, the central need for the information, and privacy. Id. Another court in this District selected the stricter modified approach and found a broad request insufficient even under reasonableness. ForceX, Inc. v. Technology Fusion, LLC, No. 4:11-cv-88, 2011 WL 2560110, at *4–5 (E.D. Va. June 27, 2011), ECF No. 22 at 8–9 & n.3. Plaintiff has developed the full modified framework above and independently asks the Court to exercise its Rule 26(d)(1) discretion for the following reasons.

Concrete claim and central need. Part VIII.C states the claim-specific showing and Part VIII.F the relevance. The answers test the original-name and account-reporting relationships in the alleged sequence and Meta’s position that the letters supplied the requested discovery. Specificity and burden. Exhibit A fixes the submission window and the original-record definitions and requests only the permitted responses and the qualification necessary for accuracy. Alternatives and timing. Plaintiff’s own naming knowledge, the letters, the public filings, and preservation do not supply the original reporting facts. Privacy. Reporting information is sensitive. The requests disclose no narrative, images, metadata, submitter identity, or other report contents, beyond the defined affirmative, negative, or undetermined proposition.

The claim connection, the present need, the absence of an equivalent answer, the limited disclosure, and the accommodation of any demonstrated response burden supply good cause. This is an additional ground for the same relief.

IX.	OBTAINING ANSWERS AND USING THEM ARE SEPARATE QUESTIONS

The relief sought is authorization under Rule 26(d)(1), and the declaration is evidence for this application under Rule 43(c) and 28 U.S.C. § 1746. Goines v. Valley Community Services Board, 822 F.3d 159, 167–68 (4th Cir. 2016), requires attention to the purpose for which a challenged document is used; the letters show what was said without making their contested statements true. Any later use of outside matters on the dismissal motions is governed by Rule 12(d); neither this declaration nor discovery authorization automatically amends the FAC or converts those motions.
